text:
Recent work supports separating observed feedback from inferred dissatisfaction. The [2024 Dagstuhl recommender-evaluation report](https://evazangerle.at/publication/bauer-dagstuhl-2024/bauer-dagstuhl-2024.pdf) emphasizes that unobserved interactions mix missing preferences with genuine negatives, and that predictive accuracy alone does not establish user satisfaction. Applied here: distinguish unidentified items, insufficient information, explicit rejection, and specific rejection reasons. Similar titles can flag possible redundancy; they do not establish ownership, incompatibility, or dislike. Those conclusions require explicit feedback or directly supporting evidence.

[From Noise to Nuance (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.hcinlp-1.20/) recommends pilot annotation, recording evidence behind labels, and examining disagreements rather than automatically treating them as noise. A suitable audit would attach each relevance or duplication label to an item ID, title/description passage, history entry, or explicit feedback statement. Independently double-annotate a shared sample; report agreement by reason, raw agreement plus a chance-corrected statistic, label frequencies, and unresolved disagreements. These are proposed operational choices, rather than a validated recommendation-specific rubric.

[Knowing When Not to Answer (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14189) studies evidence-based support/refutation/abstention in scientific reasoning and finds abstention useful for controlling errors. Its application to recommendation annotation is an extrapolation: allow “insufficient evidence” when ownership, compatibility, or intent is unknown, and report annotation coverage alongside agreement. Keep the twenty-user panel descriptive, presenting evidence-linked examples and counts; retain macro validation HR@10 as the model-selection criterion.
